$SPY remains constructive as long as it holds the $747 area, even while semiconductor stocks continue to lose momentum.

$QQQ appears less convincing, but if it can hold $718 and reclaim $726, the chart improves considerably. Failure to do so would likely lead to increasingly sloppy price action.

The major indexes for now have stayed resilient thanks to rotation into other areas of the market, but you should pay close attention to whether that support begins to crack.

*

The biggest shift is happening in semiconductors. 

Stocks like $MU $SNDK that had been rewarding every dip buyer are no longer acting like market leaders. 

Instead of automatically buying weakness, you should begin thinking in terms of selling rallies, respecting stop losses, and avoiding oversized positions. 

The leadership can quickly change and preserving capital becomes more important than hoping for a rebound.

As both $MU $SNDK approach their 50-day moving averages, shorts should avoid pressing into support and instead be prepared for tactical bounce opportunities.

*

Meanwhile, capital appears to be rotating into large-cap tech.

$AMZN continues to stand out as one of the strongest charts while chip stocks struggle. 

I remain long Amazon calls and think that the stock simply needs to stay above the $247 area to keep its bullish setup intact, with a move toward $249.50 becoming increasingly possible if buyers remain in control.

*

I also think that $SPCX has reached an important decision point.

Despite joining $QQQ and receiving bullish analyst coverage with $300 PT, the stock has failed to build strong upside momentum. 

The $155 area has become a critical decision point. 

If #SPCX can hold that level, confidence may return and the chart could stabilize. If it breaks below support, however, many recent buyers could become uncomfortable, forcing underwriters to work harder to maintain an orderly market as additional shares come to market.

*

So, this is no longer a market where every former leader deserves blind confidence.

Leadership is rotating, sector strength is shifting, and successful traders must adapt rather than rely on what worked a few months ago.

Protecting capital, respecting technical levels, and following the strongest relative strength names remain the keys to navigating the current environment.

*
